qs.q: A teenager presents with numerous gray-white, flat-topped papules with rough, pebble-like surfaces on the dorsal hands. These lesions are caused by a human papillomavirus. What is the mechanism by which low-risk HPV subtypes drive the formation of these warts?
o: Directly binding IgE molecules on cutaneous mast cells to trigger immediate degranulation
Causing an inherited deficiency of C1 esterase inhibitor and localized complement activation
Chemically modifying self-proteins to stimulate delayed-type hypersensitivity via Langerhans cells
Expression of E6 and E7 oncoproteins leading to dysregulated epidermal growth and cell survival
qs.e: Low-risk HPV subtypes express E6 and E7 oncoproteins that dysregulate epidermal cell growth and increase cell survival, resulting in warts. IgE binding is the mechanism for Type I hypersensitivity reactions in urticaria.
qs.s: Pathology of Acute Skin Inflammation: Urticaria & Eczema: MCQs

qs.q: In the histological examination of a verruca vulgaris, which cellular change is indicative of Human Papillomavirus infection in the superficial epidermal layers?
qs.e: Koilocytosis, defined as cytoplasmic vacuolization with halos of pallor around nuclei, is a hallmark histological feature of HPV-induced warts. Acantholysis involves loss of adhesion, spongiosis is intercellular edema, and dyskeratosis is premature keratinization.
qs.s: Pathology of Acute Skin Inflammation: Urticaria & Eczema: MCQs

qs.q: High-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) causes cervical carcinoma by integrating into the host genome and producing specific viral proteins. Which viral proteins are responsible for inactivating host p53 and Rb tumor suppressor proteins?
qs.e: HPV produces E6 and E7 proteins that bind to and inactivate host p53 and Rb tumor suppressor proteins, driving carcinogenesis. Reverse transcriptase and integrase are enzymes associated with retroviruses like HIV.
qs.s: Virology & Mycology: Interferons, Vaccines, Fungi, Mycetoma: MCQs

qs.q: A patient is infected with a high-risk human papillomavirus genotype known to be a major risk factor for cervical cancer. Which specific genotypes are responsible?
qs.e: High-risk HPV types 16 and 18 are strongly linked to cervical cancer. Types 6 and 11 typically cause benign common or genital warts rather than malignancy.
qs.s: Essential Medical Virology: Structure, Classification & Replication: MCQs

qs.q: High-risk strains of human papillomavirus are strongly implicated in the pathogenesis of cervical cancer. Which cellular mechanism is primarily responsible for the oncogenic potential of these viral types?
o: Viral enzymes degrade host mitochondrial membranes to induce lysis
Viral oncoprotein E6 inactivates p53 while E7 inactivates Rb
Viral integration directly upregulates host telomerase activity
Viral capsid proteins bind directly to nuclear hormone receptors
qs.e: High-risk HPV oncogenic types 16 and 18 produce E6 and E7 proteins that respectively inactivate p53 and Rb tumor suppressor genes, leading to uncontrolled cell proliferation. This specific inactivation is the key driver of HPV-mediated carcinogenesis.
qs.s: Medical Virology Semester 3 Crash Revision: MCQs

qs.q: Which specific high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) viral oncoprotein directly targets and degrades the tumor suppressor protein p53?
qs.e: The HPV E6 protein binds and degrades the p53 tumor suppressor, leading to a loss of apoptosis and DNA damage response. Conversely, the E7 protein targets the retinoblastoma (RB) protein.
qs.s: Female & Male Genital Pathology: Ulcers, HPV, Endometriosis,: MCQs

qs.q: A clinical epidemiologist is studying malignant tumors of the head and neck and notes an increasing incidence of a specific malignancy driven by human papillomavirus type 16. How does this viral-induced oropharyngeal cancer compare epidemiologically to cervical cancer?
o: It is diagnosed earlier through routine smears
It has a lower recurrence rate after therapy
It is predicted to exceed cervical rates
qs.e: HPV-driven oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma has risen sharply and is projected to surpass the incidence of cervical cancer. Routine screening smears are standard for the cervix but do not exist for the oropharynx.

qs.q: When examining risk factors for cervical carcinoma, pathologists emphasize the role of specific high-risk human papillomavirus genotypes. Which viral proteins directly degrade p53 and Rb tumor suppressor proteins?
qs.e: High-risk HPV types 16 and 18 produce E6 and E7 viral proteins that bind and degrade host p53 and Rb tumour suppressors, driving carcinogenesis. L1 and L2 are structural capsid proteins.
qs.s: Medical Pathology Final Revision: Chemical, Hema, Systemic: MCQs

es.q: A patient with a history of recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (RRP) inquires about its cause and transmission in children. Identify the specific Human Papillomavirus (HPV) types responsible for RRP and describe its mode of transmission in children.
es.m: Recurrent Respiratory Papillomatosis (RRP) is caused by HPV types 6 and 11. In children, it is transmitted via vertical transmission during delivery.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Human papillomavirus (HPV) is a DNA virus that infects epithelial cells, causing warts and, for high‑risk types, precancerous lesions that can progress to cancer. Persistent infection of the cervical transformation zone is the key step in oncogenesis.

sections.p: HPV is a small, non‑enveloped double‑stranded DNA virus that infects basal epithelial cells after micro‑abrasion. Low‑risk types (6, 11) cause benign warts; high‑risk types (16, 18, 45, 31, 33, 52, 58) can lead to dysplasia and cancer.
b: DNA virus, 8 kb genome
Infects skin and mucosal epithelium
Transmission: sexual contact, perinatal, fomites

sections.p: HPV capsid proteins L1 and L2 form the outer shell; early proteins (E1‑E7) drive replication and oncogenesis. E6 degrades p53; E7 inactivates Rb, allowing uncontrolled cell division.
b: High‑risk types express E6/E7 oncogenes
Low‑risk types lack strong oncogenic activity

sections.p: Virus enters through micro‑abrasions, reaches basal layer, replicates as cells differentiate, and is shed in skin or mucosal secretions. Latent infection can persist for years.
b: Sexual contact is main route
Perinatal transmission can cause respiratory papillomatosis
Fomite spread possible but less common

sections.p: Low‑risk HPV produces condylomata acuminata (genital warts). High‑risk HPV causes cervical intra‑epithelial neoplasia (CIN) that can progress to invasive cervical cancer; also anal, penile, vulvar, vaginal, and oropharyngeal cancers.
b: CIN grades 1‑3 based on histology
High‑risk HPV infection is necessary but not sufficient for cancer
Co‑factors: HIV, smoking, immunosuppression

sections.p: Screening combines cytology (Pap smear) and HPV DNA testing. Histology confirms CIN grade. In low‑resource settings, visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) is used.

t.b: Detects abnormal squamous cells; ASC-US or higher prompts HPV testing or colposcopy
Identifies presence of oncogenic types; positive with normal cytology indicates need for surveillance
Provides definitive histologic grade; guides treatment
Detects acetowhite lesions in settings without cytology; positive result leads to cryotherapy or referral

sections.p: Management targets the lesion and prevents progression. Low‑risk warts are treated locally; high‑risk precancers are excised or ablated. Vaccination prevents infection.
b: Cryotherapy or topical imiquimod for genital warts
Loop electrosurgical excision (LEEP) for CIN 2‑3
HPV vaccine (bivalent, quadrivalent, nonavalent) given before sexual debut

sections.p: Key points to remember for exams.
b: High‑risk HPV types 16/18 cause ~70% of cervical cancers
E6/E7 oncoproteins inactivate p53 and Rb
Screening: Pap + HPV co‑test every 5 years after 30 y

whenToSeekHelp: Persistent genital warts, especially large or bleeding
Abnormal Pap smear or positive high‑risk HPV test
Unexplained pelvic pain, bleeding, or mass

faq.q: Can HPV infection be cleared without treatment?
faq.a: Yes, most low‑risk infections clear spontaneously; high‑risk infections may persist and need monitoring.

faq.q: Is the HPV vaccine useful after infection?
faq.a: Vaccination protects against types not yet acquired and is still recommended even after prior infection.

faq.q: Why are HIV‑positive patients at higher risk for HPV‑related cancer?
faq.a: Immunosuppression reduces clearance of high‑risk HPV, increasing persistence and progression.
